items.excerpt: ## Huge plumes of black smoke billowed over St Petersburg, Russia’s second-largest city, on Sunday, 18 October, as a large-scale Ukrainian drone attack sparked fires at industrial and logistics facilities. Russian officials said 126 drones had been intercepted in the surrounding region. ... Footage shared on social media showed a major blaze at a warehouse operated by Ozon, Russia's second-largest online retailer, which said its logistics centre had been struck. Other images showed thick smoke rising from the area of the St Petersburg Oil Terminal, while an oil refinery and depot were also reportedly hit. St Petersburg's governor, Alexander Beglov, confirmed that air-defence systems had been activated after a large-scale Ukrainian drone attack on the city overnight, while Leningrad Region governor Alexander Drozdenko initially reported that 126 drones had been shot down over the surrounding region. He later raised that figure to 144, with some reports putting it at 145. The assault set the Petersburg Oil Terminal and the Ruchyi oil depot alight and struck infrastructure in several districts of the city. Beglov said one person was killed and five others were injured, while operations at Pulkovo Airport were temporarily restricted for safety reasons. The strikes came as President Volodymyr Zelensky announced that Ukraine would resume attacks on Russian oil refineries after briefly suspending them following Donald Trump’s declaration of an “energy ceasefire” on 11 October. Neither side formally confirmed the arrangement, and Zelensky accused Russia of carrying out 76 attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure over the following week, including strikes on substations in four regions that left tens of thousands of families without power. The latest exchange underlines the continuing struggle over energy infrastructure, with both sides treating refineries, terminals and power grids

items.title: Inflation is retreating from most of the store — why your biggest bills are the holdouts: Chart of the Day
items.excerpt: Inflation is retreating from most of the store — why your biggest bills are the holdouts: Chart of the Day # Inflation is retreating from most of the store — why your biggest bills are the holdouts: Chart of the Day Jared Blikre Sun, October 18, 2026 at 6:33 AM CDT 3 min read Inflation is reaching fewer corners of the economy. That doesn't mean life is getting cheaper. Only about 38% of the roughly 175 categories in the Consumer Price Index rose faster than a 3% annual pace over the past six months, according to Yahoo Finance calculations from Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) data. That's down from 56% in May and the fewest since spring 2025. The count borrows a test from Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, who laid it out at Jackson Hole in August. He counts how many categories in the Fed's preferred PCE price gauge are rising faster than 3%, a gauge of how widespread inflation is. The Fed's goal is still 2%. BLS, Yahoo Finance "Too many categories are still posting increases above 3% on both a six- and 12-month basis," Warsh said after the Fed raised rates in September. By that yardstick, September looked better than its hotter-than-expected headline. The 12-month count slipped to about 47% from 51% in August. At the 2022 peak, about 4 in 5 categories topped 3%. In the two decades before the pandemic, about 1 in 3 typically did. A narrower spread strengthens the case for waiting, and traders have leaned that way. The bond market put the odds of a hike at the Oct. 27-28 meeting at about 17% by Friday's close, according to Bloomberg data — down from roughly 33% after Wednesday's CPI report. Warsh declined to preview his next move in remarks Friday before the International Monetary Fund. Some Fed officials want more evidence before moving. Chicago Fed President Austan Goolsbee called September's inflation report discouraging but told Yahoo Finance's Jennifer Schonberger he favors waiting before acting again. "We need to get more data," he said. ## The holdout categories are the expensive ones Electricity, rent, hospital services, and car repairs have all been rising faster than 3% over the past six months, after adjusting for seasonal swings. Gasoline is up about 34% from a year ago. Together, the categories still above the line make up at least 60% of the CPI basket, which the BLS weights by how much households spend on each item. Groceries show the other side of the problem. Grocery prices rose less than 2% over the past year, yet they're still up nearly a third since December 2019. Electricity is up 43% over the same stretch. BLS, Yahoo Finance Slower inflation means prices rise more slowly. It doesn't bring them back down, and the Fed has no intention of returning to 2019 prices. Not everyone sees progress. "There is little evidence of a cooling or a broad-based disinflationary impulse," RSM chief economist Joe Brusuelas wrote Wednesday, pointing to trade, energy, and AI as sources of stubborn price pressure. He expects another quarter-point hike in December. The bond market leans his way on the longer view. Traders still price in about one full quarter-point increase by the Dec. 9 meeting and nearly three by September 2027. The next test arrives Oct. 29, when September PCE inflation is released, one day after the Fed decides. Next month's CPI report follows. If the six-month count holds below 40%, the case for waiting gets stronger. A return to 50% or more — near where it sat for most of the first half of the year — would put a hike back on the table. Watch rent and electricity. Until they cool, a shrinking count won't feel like relief. *Internal AI tools helped analyze interview transcripts, research, and draft this post. Humans reviewed, edited, and fact-checked this post before publication.* *Jared Blikre is the global markets and data editor for Yahoo Finance. Follow him on X at @SPYJared or email him at **jaredblikre@yahooinc.com**.*

items.excerpt: Retail price impacts from the Iran war are uneven but add up for US households before midterms NEW YORK (AP) — High fuel prices are making it more expensive to drive, fly and buy some goods more than seven months into the U.S.-Iran war. That's prolonging the strain on American households as the midterm elections approach., The chief economist at Moody’s Analytics estimates the war has cost the average U.S. household the equivalent of almost $2,000, including $1,100 related to energy. Motorists and airline passengers so far have borne the clearest consequences from disrupted Middle East oil shipments. The elevated cost of making and moving goods hasn't translated into across-the-board retail price increases. Shoppers may not be spared indefinitely, though. U.S. consumers are uneasy about the increasingly high-tech ways that restaurant chains and major retailers are setting prices. Digital price tags are replacing paper ones in grocery aisles. Artificial intelligence tools help businesses decide what to charge by predicting how customers might respond. Terms like “dynamic pricing” and “surveillance pricing” are stirring up anger and anxiety on social media. Much of the concern focuses on whether customer data is getting used to give different people different prices for the same product. Walmart and McDonald's say critics misunderstand how their pricing tools work. Lawmakers and regulators are taking preemptive action to restrict when companies can use personal data in pricing. items.title: Harry Styles Enlists John Wilson for Documentary About MSG Residency
items.excerpt: Harry Styles Enlists John Wilson for Documentary About MSG Residency # Harry Styles Enlists John Wilson for Documentary About Madison Square Garden Residency The History of Concrete documentarian has been quietly filming singer's historic Together, Together residency since August By Daniel Kreps Contact Daniel Kreps on X Contact Daniel Kreps by Email (tips@rollingstone.com) October 18, 2026 Harry Styles Hollywood To You/Star Max/GC Images Harry Styles has enlisted filmmaker John Wilson to make a documentary about the singer’s current Madison Square Garden residency. In recent days, photos of Wilson — the offbeat documentarian behind his own *How To With John Wilson* HBO series and *The History of Concrete* — trailing Styles with camera in hand emerged on social media, leading fans to wonder if the two were collaborating on some sort of project. > Harry out and about in New York today – October 16 (via People) pic.twitter.com/kY6LhqEPNP > — HSD💋🪩 (@hsdaily) October 16, 2026 *Variety* has confirmed that the project in question is a documentary about Styles’ Together, Together 30-show residency at MSG, which started in August — when Wilson began filming — and runs through October 31. Not a traditional documentarian, Wilson’s Styles film will feature “a hybrid of live performances and a glimpse into Styles’ world,” *Variety* reported, adding that Wilson will dig deep into the residency with “authentic human stories of everyone involved in the tour —from the singer and his fans to countless others behind the scenes.” Universal Pictures Content Group, Peanut World Pictures and Styles are producing the documentary, with a theatrical release potentially in the works. In the grand tradition of Martin Scorsese’s *The Last Waltz* and Jonathan Demme’s *Stop Making Sense*, Wilson is the latest high-profile filmmaker to helm a musician’s concert film in recent months: David Byrne recruited *The Brutalist* director Brady Corbet to film his Baltimore concert in 70mm, and Cameron Winter’s Carnegie Hall concert was captured live by Paul Thomas Anderson (with help from Benny Safdie). items.title: Tini: FUTTURA World Tour | Miami & Miami Beach
items.excerpt: Argentine pop artist Tini brings her FUTTURA World Tour to downtown Miami for the tour’s only U.S. stop. Tini: FUTTURA World Tour takes place Sunday, October 18, 2026 at Kaseya Center. The tour is described as a retrospective project spanning Tini’s different musical eras, from her early international breakthrough on Disney Channel Latin America’s Violetta to her solo career in pop, urbano, cumbia and alternative pop. The Miami concert follows the tour’s launch in Buenos Aires and brings the arena production to a U.S. audience for one night only. Born Martina Stoessel, Tini is an Argentine singer, actress and performer whose albums include Tini, Quiero Volver, Tini Tini Tini, Cupido and Un Mechón de Pelo. Her career includes chart success in Latin America and Europe, multiple major music awards and collaborations that have expanded her reach across Latin pop and global music audiences. The event is open to all ages, though ages 18 and older are recommended.

items.title: John Carpenter, Charlize Theron, Receive Academy Museum Gala Honors
items.excerpt: The Academy Museum has announced three honorees for its sixth annual fundraising gala: John Carpenter, Charlize Theron, and Colman Domingo. The gala is set to take place on Saturday, October 17, with Steven Spielberg, Robert Rodriguez, and Kate Capshaw serving as the event’s co-chairs. ... Carpenter, a legendary genre filmmaker who changed the horror industry forever with “Halloween” and went on to direct hits like “The Thing,” “Escape from New York,” “They Live,” and “Big Trouble in Little China,” will receive the Luminary Award. Theron, the Oscar-winning star of “Monster” whose penchant for physical transformations has given her a filmography that includes everything from “Mad Max: Fury Road” to “The Odyssey,” will receive the Icon Award. Domingo, the prolific actor with an Emmy win and two Oscar and Tony nominations, is set to receive the Vantage Award.
